sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **The main image and the headline don't make one idea together.** The picture at about x 96–656, y 220–420 is flat blocks: a pale grey rectangle, a dark grey slab, a pale blue band and a blue rounded bar. None of it shows what the headline and body promise: wider ramps, a covered waiting area, benches facing the water, a kiosk. The caption says "The new north landing, seen from the water at low tide", but the picture doesn't show that either. It takes about a quarter of the content column and adds nothing the words haven't said, so a reader can't see the rebuild for themselves. There's also a side cost. The blue rounded bar at about x 496–606, y 340–364 is the same blue and corner radius as the Sign up button at x 789–888, y 293–337, so it reads as a second button. The eye catches on it and some readers may try to click it. This is my own judgment as a designer; the catalog entry has no approved source. Fix: use a real photo or a drawing that shows the ramp meeting the deck, ideally with a pram or wheelchair on it, so the picture proves the second paragraph's claim. If it stays an illustration, take the interface blue and the button shape out of it. Mark: defect. Weight: major. It's the only evidence on the page for the news, and the bar competes with the one real action.

Also worth passing on, though no line in this section covers it: the form asks only for "Your name" and "Home landing" (y 143–277). The note below says "We send one short note when the timetable changes" but never says where. With no email or phone field, a stranger can't tell how the note would reach them, and as shown the form can't deliver what it promises. Fix: add the contact field, or say in the note where it goes. Mark: defect. Weight: major for the signup. The interface critic should own this.

**What's working.**
- **Clear purpose.** The headline "Landing stage rebuild" and the two short paragraphs make the page's purpose clear at once. The closing line "prams and wheelchairs roll straight on" says what the rebuild means for the passenger instead of only describing it.
- **One quiet mood.** One sans-serif family, one blue and soft greys give a calm, public-service tone that suits a ferry operator's notice.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (main image and headline make one idea), 0 unsure

I couldn't run the crop and entries scripts because Bash was denied. The image is one screen (1280×800), so I worked from the whole image and read the entries directly. All sizes below are estimates by eye, not measurements.

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?**
   - **Where:** The form labels "Your name" and "Home landing" (about x 789–860, y 137–230) look like about 13 px in a thin grey weight. The helper note under "Sign up" (y 355–390), the figure caption (y 444) and the footer line (y 750) look like about 12 px in the same thin grey.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The labels look almost the same as the fine print, so the form has no separate "label" level. In the card, "Your name" reads like the reassurance note below the button, and the field names, which are what the viewer has to act on, are no stronger than the small print. Because the weight is thin as well, the whole small level looks faint rather than just secondary.
   - **Why:** A hierarchy needs two to four levels that each differ clearly from the next ("Visual hierarchy has distinct levels", Müller-Brockmann; Lupton). Sizes a point apart read as accidents, not as different levels (Bringhurst).
   - **Fix:** Either merge labels and fine print into one deliberate small size, or set the labels apart by weight or colour (regular or medium weight, darker ink) rather than by another size. Keep the caption, helper note and footer as the single small detail size.
   - **Kind and weight:** Convention. Minor: the page is short and the form has only two fields.

**What's working.**
- **The title clearly leads.** "Landing stage rebuild" (about 32 px bold, near-black) is the biggest and darkest text on the page, so the eye knows where to start. The card heading "Get timetable changes" (about 22 px bold) is a clear step down, so the sign-up box reads as secondary to the article and doesn't compete with it.
- **Headings and body differ in weight as well as size.** Both headings are bold over regular body text. The card heading and the body are only about 4 px apart, but they still read as separate levels, so the scale stays small without blurring.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Exact type sizes and contrast of the thin grey small text. Measure them in the live page to confirm the labels and fine print are as close as they look.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (text levels distinct: form labels and fine print look almost the same size and weight).

I critiqued only the arrangement section. One process note: running commands was refused, so I couldn't crop the image or run the entries script. The image is 1280×800 (about one screen), so I worked from the whole image and read the reference file directly to check the entries.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Do only related elements look alike, with no accidental groups or shapes formed between unrelated ones?"** In the illustration (Figure 1, x≈96–656, y≈220–420), the blue rounded bar at about x 496–606, y 340–364 seems to be the boat. It is the same saturated blue as the Sign up button (x≈789–888, y≈293–337) and has the same small corner radius and roughly the same proportions. It is also the only strong colour in the picture. So it looks like a second button, and some viewers will try to click the picture or wonder why there are two calls to action. Like shapes and colours are read as one group (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II "Shape", grouping by similarity). Keep the action blue only on things you can click: give the boat a colour from the picture's own muted palette, or a hull shape that doesn't read as a pill. Defect. Weight: minor.
2. **"Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid, so column lines and gutters repeat down the page?"** The figure's right edge is at x≈656, but the body text in the same column runs further right: "small kiosk sells" ends at about x 683, and the first line at about x 660. So the paragraph hangs about 25–30 px past the picture. The picture looks like it has a fixed width and isn't set to the column. The left column ends up with no clear right edge, and the gap to the card changes from about 77 px beside the text to about 104 px beside the picture. Images should take their width from the column (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "The photograph in the grid system"). Set the figure to the full width of the text column, or narrow the text column to match the figure, so the two share one right edge. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **Clear grouping by space.** Inside the card, each label sits about 8 px above its field and about 20 px below the field before it, and the card has even inner padding of about 28 px. In the article, the caption sits closer to its figure than to the next paragraph. Every group reads without any rules.
- **Asymmetric two-column layout.** The roughly 600 px article column and the roughly 360 px form card follow the order of the content: the story first, then the sign-up. The bordered card on the right balances the darker headline and picture on the left, and nothing is centred out of habit.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** How the card and the article column stack on narrow screens: whether the form ends up before or after the story. It matters here because the sign-up is the page's only action.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (one grid for all blocks, pictures included; only related elements look alike)

**Section.** Text: applies. The text is a news-style heading, two body paragraphs, a figure caption, form labels with helper text, and a footer note. I assumed this is a ferry service page about a rebuilt landing, with a sign-up for timetable changes. Bash was refused, so I couldn't make close-up crops or open the reference entries through the script. I judged everything from the whole 1280×800 image.

**Findings**
1. **Is small text set in a weight heavy enough to hold up, with hairline weights kept to large sizes?** No. All the small text looks like a light or thin cut at about 12–13 px:
   - the caption "Figure 1. The new north landing…" (about x 96, y 444)
   - the field labels "Your name" and "Home landing" (about x 789, y 143 and y 223)
   - the helper text "We send one short note…" (about x 789, y 362–382)
   - the footer note (about x 96, y 750)

   Thin strokes at that size break up on screen and look grey and faint even if the colour itself passes contrast. The caption and helper text fade into the background, and the field labels look weaker than the input borders they sit above. These labels are the only thing telling the viewer what to type, and the helper text is the promise about how many notes they'll get. This is my own judgment, not a cited source: I couldn't open the entry, so I'm citing nothing. The fix is to use the regular (400) weight of the same family for every size below about 14 px and keep light weights for large display type. Measure contrast in a live browser once the weight changes. Defect. Weight: minor, though it sits on the form the page is asking people to fill in.

**What's working.**
- **Body text.** The first paragraph is set at about 17 px with roughly 66 characters to the line and generous line spacing. It is flush left with an even rag, and each paragraph ends on a full phrase, so it reads at a comfortable pace.
- **One type plan.** A single sans family carries everything. Bold sets the headings apart ("Landing stage rebuild" at about 34 px, "Get timetable changes" at about 22 px) and regular sets the reading text, so each size has a clear job.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the caption and helper text actually reach 4.5:1 contrast once the thin strokes are anti-aliased. Measure the rendered colour in a browser; without crops I couldn't zoom in.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (small text in a weight heavy enough).

sections.report:
**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is each status color (red, green, amber, blue) used only for its usual meaning to this audience?** In the figure, a rounded rectangle at about x 496–606, y 340–364 (it stands for the ferry on the water) is drawn in the same saturated blue as the "Sign up" button (789–888, 293–337), with the same rounded corners and about the same height. Nothing else on the page uses that blue, so the page has taught the viewer that this blue means "press me". The shape in the picture then looks like a second button, and some viewers may try to click it or look for a label on it. It also pulls the eye into the figure before the real call to action. The source here is Apple, *Human Interface Guidelines: Color*: keep a set color meaning and don't reuse it for unrelated decoration. Apple's guidance to keep interactive colors off elements you can't interact with applies even more strongly. Fix: give the boat a colour that belongs to the illustration, such as a darker or greyer blue, or a different hue from the figure's palette. Changing its shape so it no longer reads as a pill would also help. Keep the saturated blue for the button only. Convention. Weight: minor, because the caption and the figure frame make a mistaken click unlikely.

**What's working.**
- Structure comes from light and dark, not from hue. The near-black headline and body, the dark grey deck, and the pale blue-grey sky and water would keep the page readable in greyscale. The figure separates from the white page without a border.
- The palette is small and calm: neutrals, pale cool tints, and one saturated blue covering a tiny share of the area. That lets the button stand out as the one strong colour without having to compete.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 8 yes, 1 no (status color used only for its usual meaning), 0 unsure

Walk (working notes): The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image. Bash was refused, so I could not run the crop script. Pictures: one figure, a flat block illustration at x 96–656, y 220–420.
- Shows its content, no placeholder: **no**. It reads as a wireframe placeholder, not the landing the caption names.
- Full quality: yes. Crop intended: yes. Figure-ground: yes. One style: yes (single picture). Photos consistent: yes (none). Icons consistent: yes (none). One viewpoint/light: yes (flat side view, no light). Texture restraint: yes (none). No fake depth: yes. Logo clear space: yes (no logo). Mark simple: yes (none).

The one `no` has no catalog entry, so I judged it on common sense and opened no entries.

**Section.** Pictures: applies. There is one figure (Figure 1) at about x 96–656, y 220–420.

**Findings**
1. **Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box?** Where: Figure 1, at x 96–656, y 220–420.
   - **What the viewer sees:** a pale sky band, a light grey box, a dark grey slab and a blue rounded bar over a flat blue strip. It looks like a wireframe placeholder, not a picture of a place.
   - **Why it fails:** the caption promises "the new north landing, seen from the water at low tide". The text around it talks about wider ramps, a covered waiting area, benches facing the water, a kiosk, and ramps that meet the deck at every tide. The picture shows none of these. A reader can't tell which block is the stage, the shelter or the boat, and nothing shows a ramp meeting a deck.
   - **Extra problem with the blue bar:** the bar at about x 496–606, y 340–364 is the same blue as the "Sign up" button (x 789–888, y 293–337), with the same rounded corners. So it reads as a stray UI button sitting in the picture, not as a boat or a pontoon.
   - **Cost:** the figure takes about a quarter of the content column and adds nothing. The one claim a picture could prove, step-free boarding for prams and wheelchairs, goes unshown.
   - **What would make it fine:** if this is a stand-in for a photo that hasn't been placed yet, it should be swapped before shipping. Otherwise, show the real landing: a photo, or an illustration with enough detail to see the ramp, the shelter and the waterline. The boat or pontoon should not use the interface's button colour or shape.
   - Kind and weight: defect, common sense (no catalog entry). Major.

**What's working.** The figure's palette of pale blue, greys and muted water blue stays quiet next to the text and the sign-up card. It doesn't fight the headline or the form. The caption sits close under the image in a smaller size, so it clearly belongs to the picture.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether this is the intended artwork or a placeholder left in by mistake (a missing asset or a load fallback). Check the live page or the source asset.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (every image shows its content, no placeholder)

**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. There is no chart, table of figures, dashboard or headline number. The only picture is Figure 1, a flat drawing of the landing seen from the water (96–656 × 220–420). It is a picture, not a data display, so it belongs to the pictures section.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. There is one sign-up form on the right, with two text fields and a "Sign up" button.

**Findings**
1. **Is everything the user needs to act visible on this screen, with nothing to remember from another?** The form card (about x 760–1120, y 56–420) asks for "Your name" and "Home landing" and then says "We send one short note when the timetable changes." It never asks for an email address or a phone number, and it never says how the note will arrive. A visitor filling it in can't tell where the notes will go. Either they give up, or they press "Sign up" expecting a later step that may not come. The form can't do its one job as shown. Nielsen 6 (recognition rather than recall) is the closest catalog line, but this is mostly common sense: the form leaves out the one field it needs. Fix: add a labelled field for where the note goes, such as "Email" or "Mobile number", and name that channel in the note under the button ("We email you one short note…"). If the name isn't used for anything, drop it so the form stays at two fields. **Defect. Major.**
2. **Do the inputs allow only valid values, by pickers, input types, or disabled options?** "Home landing" (field at about x 790–1090, y 237–276) is an open text box. The landings are a short, fixed list, so people will type spellings, abbreviations or landings that don't exist, and the service can't match them to a route. Nielsen 5 (error prevention) and Norman (constraints) both apply. Fix: make it a dropdown or a set of radio buttons listing the landings, ideally with the nearest or most common one pre-selected. **Defect. Minor**: it hurts how reliable the data is, but not whether people can sign up.
3. **Are required or optional fields marked?** Neither field says whether it is required (labels at y 143 and y 223). With only two fields the cost is small. It grows once the contact field from finding 1 is added and the name may become optional. Fix: mark the optional field "(optional)", or say "All fields required" above the form. **Convention. Minor.**

**What's working.**
- The single filled blue "Sign up" button (about 99×44 px at x 789–888, y 293–337) is clearly the only action, it is large enough to hit, and it sits directly under the fields it submits. There's no doubt about what to press.
- Each label sits above its own field, much closer to it (about 14 px) than to the field above (about 26 px). The fields have dark, solid borders that clearly read as input boxes.
- The reassurance line under the button ("one short note… You can stop the notes at any time") is useful help placed exactly where someone decides whether to commit, and it is honest. Nothing is pre-checked and there's no hidden opt-in.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- The focus ring on the two fields and the button. Check in a browser that it is at least 2 px thick and has at least 3:1 contrast.
- What happens after "Sign up": the confirmation, and the error messages for an empty or invalid field (do they name the field and say how to fix it?).

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 3 no (everything needed to act visible; inputs allow only valid values; required or optional fields marked), 1 unsure (focus indicator).
